adversarial.note: every word is a rotation of the same 10-letter multiset, so all n words share one anagram signature (one exact dict key, not merely one hash bucket) and land in a single group; empirically this does NOT degrade to O(n^2) the way distinct-but-colliding keys do, since CPython dicts resolve a repeated exact key by direct slot lookup rather than probing a chain — see README

complexity.correctness_reason: The return annotation `tuple(int)` is a function call evaluated at definition time, and since `int` is not iterable it raises TypeError ('type' object is not iterable), so the module fails to load on every permitted input.
complexity.notes: The two-pass construction recomputes every signature twice; a single pass with dict.setdefault or a collections.defaultdict(list) would be cleaner and half the hashing work. The intended annotation was presumably tuple[int, ...] rather than the call tuple(int).
complexity.summary: Computes a 26-element character-count tuple as the anagram signature for each word, builds a dict mapping signatures to groups, then appends each word to its group in a second pass and returns the dict's values.

complexity.notes: Recursion adds O(log n) stack space where an iterative loop would be O(1), and Python's default recursion limit (~1000) would be exceeded for astronomically large n; an iterative version avoids both.
complexity.summary: Standard recursive binary search: each call halves the search interval [start, end) until the target is found or the interval is empty.

complexity.notes: Using mid = start + (end - start) // 2 and a half-open interval is clean and avoids off-by-one errors; the empty-array case is also handled correctly by the start == end check.
complexity.summary: Classic iterative binary search over the half-open interval [start, end), narrowing the range each iteration and returning the index on equality; after the loop at most one candidate remains and it is checked explicitly. The final guard handles both the exhausted (start == end) case and a lone non-matching element.

complexity.notes: best_buy is dead code — a leftover from the intended O(n) running-minimum approach; removing it (or actually using it) would clarify the solution. The initial value 100 leans on the NeetCode price cap but is harmless since the variable is unused.
complexity.summary: Brute-force: for every buy day i, scan every later sell day j and track the maximum profit, never going below 0. The best_buy variable is computed but never actually used in the profit calculation.

complexity.correctness_reason: best_buy is hard-coded to 100, so once the price cap is lifted an input like [1000, 2000] yields 1900 instead of the correct 1000.
complexity.notes: Initializing best_buy to the constant 100 instead of prices[0] or infinity is a subtle correctness hazard that only works because of the stated price cap.
complexity.summary: Single pass tracking the minimum price seen so far (best_buy) and the maximum profit of selling at each day against that minimum.

complexity.correctness_reason: Once the value caps are lifted, float division of unbounded ints loses precision (distinct times past 2^53 compare equal, merging fleets that should be separate) and can even raise OverflowError converting huge ints to float; within NeetCode's 10^6 caps the double arithmetic is exact enough to be correct.
complexity.notes: The debug print (with math.ceil) should be removed; it adds I/O per iteration and the ceil values aren't even used in the comparison. Comparing (target - p)/s as floats is fragile — cross-multiplication (target-p1)*s2 vs (target-p2)*s1 keeps everything in exact integer arithmetic.
complexity.summary: Sorts cars by position, then scans from the car nearest the target backward: a trailing car merges into the lead fleet if its arrival time is no greater than the leader's, otherwise it starts a new fleet. Arrival times are compared as floats via division.

complexity.correctness_reason: Arrival times are compared with floating-point division, which is exact enough under NeetCode's caps (target, speeds, positions <= 10^6) but with the generalized unbounded magnitudes two distinct arrival times can round to the same float and be wrongly merged into one fleet.
complexity.notes: Building the pairs via sorted(zip(position, speed)) would be cleaner than the indexed list comprehension; popping from the end keeps each step O(1). Comparing arrival times via cross-multiplication ((target - p1) * s2 vs (target - p2) * s1) would avoid floating point entirely and stay exact for arbitrarily large integers.
complexity.summary: Sorts the cars by position and scans from the car nearest the target backward, using arrival time (target - position) / speed: a car forms a new fleet only if its arrival time exceeds that of the fleet ahead, otherwise it merges into that fleet.

complexity.correctness_reason: Arrival times are compared as floats, which is exact enough only because positions, speeds, and target are capped at 10^6 (cross-products stay under 2^53); in the generalized problem, e.g. target and distances near 10^17 with speeds differing in the 17th significant digit (such as (target-p1)/s1 = 10^17/1 versus (target-p2)/s2 = (10^17+1)/1), rounding merges or splits fleets incorrectly.
complexity.notes: The O(target) counting array is an unusual substitute for simply sorting by position (O(n log n), O(n) space); the pop()-driven while loop is also less readable than an indexed loop or a monotonic stack. Under the given scaling target ~ 2n+1, so the allocation stays linear.
complexity.summary: Places each car into a counting array indexed by position, compacts it, then walks from the car nearest the target backward, merging any car whose float arrival time is at most the current lead fleet's time and counting a new fleet otherwise.

complexity.correctness_reason: Arrival times are compared with float division, which loses precision once position/target/speed magnitudes exceed about 2^53 (and overflows entirely near 1e308), so with the caps on target and speed lifted a pair of fleets whose true arrival-time ratio differs below float64 resolution can be merged or split incorrectly.
complexity.notes: Clever branch selection keeps the counting-array strategy from ever being asymptotically worse than the sort. Comparing arrival times via float division is concise but cross-multiplication ((target - p1) * s2 >= (target - p2) * s1) would be exact; also, silently initializing result to 1 relies on the n >= 1 constraint.
complexity.summary: Hybrid approach: it builds a position-indexed array when target is small relative to n log n, otherwise sorts the (position, speed) pairs. It then walks cars from nearest-to-target outward, merging each car into the lead fleet if its arrival time is no better, and counting a new fleet otherwise.

complexity.notes: Idiomatic monotonic stack; storing tuples works fine, though storing indices alone and comparing temperatures[stack[-1]] would be slightly cleaner.
complexity.summary: Monotonic decreasing stack of (temperature, index) pairs; each new temperature pops all cooler pending days and records the day difference. Each index is pushed and popped at most once, giving amortized O(1) per day.

adversarial.note: n distinct multiples of 2**61-1, all hashing to 0, so every dict insert/lookup collides

complexity.notes: Shadows the builtin name 'dict'; the counting pass and second pass are both unnecessary — a single pass with a set (or early return when a key already exists) is simpler and avoids the extra loop.
complexity.summary: Counts occurrences of each value in a dict, then scans again returning True on the first value with count greater than 1.

complexity.correctness_reason: int(a/b) routes through a double, so once intermediate values exceed 2^53 (which the generalized problem allows, e.g. dividing 200^12 by 1 after a chain of multiplications) the truncation loses exactness or overflows, whereas NeetCode's tests keep intermediates small enough for float division to be exact.
complexity.notes: The repeated if/elif chain could be replaced by a dispatch dict mapping operators to lambdas for readability. int(a/b) performs float division; a pure-integer truncating division (e.g., abs(a)//abs(b) with a sign fix, or math.trunc-free integer logic) would avoid any floating-point dependence.
complexity.summary: Classic stack evaluation of postfix notation: push parsed operands, and on each of the four operators pop the top two values, apply the operation (with truncation-toward-zero division via int(a/b)), and push the result.

complexity.notes: The bare except clause is unidiomatic and would swallow unrelated errors; comparing two collections.Counter objects (or dict.get with a default of 0) would be cleaner. The bidirectional comparison is redundant since equal multisets only need one direction plus a length check.
complexity.summary: Builds character-frequency dictionaries for both strings, then compares them in both directions, catching KeyError when a character appears in one string but not the other.

complexity.notes: s.lower() copies the whole string, making space O(n); comparing characters case-insensitively in place would give O(1) extra space. The early 'return True' when a runs off the end correctly handles strings with no remaining alphanumerics.
complexity.summary: Two-pointer scan from both ends, skipping non-alphanumeric characters and comparing lowercased characters until the pointers meet.

complexity.notes: Idiomatic and readable; allocates several intermediate strings (lower, join, reversed slice), but all are O(n). A two-pointer scan would reduce extra space to O(1).
complexity.summary: Filters the lowercased string down to alphanumeric characters, then checks whether the result equals its reverse.

complexity.notes: Reusing `largest` as both the sweep bound and the running answer is confusing but safe here because range() is materialized before the loop mutates it. Starting the sweep at i = 0 wastes one pass; range(1, largest+1) suffices.
complexity.summary: Sweeps every integer height i from 0 to max(heights), and for each i scans the array once to find the widest run of bars with height >= i, tracking the best area i * width. Correct because the optimal rectangle's height equals some bar height, but it is O(n * H) instead of the O(n) monotonic-stack solution.

complexity.correctness_reason: Depends on the stated cap of 1000 nodes: an acyclic list longer than 1005 nodes would exhaust the loop and wrongly return true.
complexity.notes: A magic constant (1005) substitutes for a real algorithm; Floyd's tortoise-and-hare or a visited set would be the idiomatic approaches.
complexity.summary: Walks the list for at most 1005 steps; if null is reached there is no cycle, otherwise it assumes a cycle exists. This exploits the statement's length cap of 1000 rather than actually detecting a cycle.

complexity.notes: Unused counter variable i can be removed. Node hashing relies on ListNode's default identity hash, which is safe here since input cannot steer object addresses into collisions.
complexity.summary: Traverses the list while storing visited nodes in a set; if a node is revisited, a cycle exists, otherwise the walk terminates at null. Uses O(n) extra space rather than the O(1)-space Floyd's tortoise-and-hare alternative.

adversarial.note: n distinct multiples of 2**61-1, all hashing to 0, so every set insert/lookup collides

complexity.notes: Works but is less idiomatic than the standard approach of iterating the set and only expanding from run starts (where x-1 is absent); the pop-and-expand-both-ways version is correct and still linear but does more membership probes per run.
complexity.summary: Builds a set of the numbers, then repeatedly pops an arbitrary element and expands both downward and upward to collect and remove its entire consecutive run, tracking the maximum run length. Each element is removed from the set exactly once, so total work is linear on average.

complexity.notes: The root-selection preamble is verbose and duplicates the comparison logic; using a dummy head node would eliminate the special-casing and make the loop uniform. Minor spacing inconsistencies (current=next1).
complexity.summary: Iterative two-pointer merge: picks the smaller head as the root, then walks both lists attaching the smaller node each step, and finally appends the non-empty remainder.

complexity.notes: Idiomatic and clean; initializing min_stack with float('inf') as a sentinel elegantly avoids empty checks in push. Each operation is worst-case O(1), satisfying the problem's requirement exactly.
complexity.summary: Maintains a main stack alongside a parallel min-stack that only pushes a value when it is less than or equal to the current minimum, so getMin is a constant-time peek at the min-stack's top. Pop mirrors the min-stack pop when the removed value equals the current minimum.

complexity.notes: The nums[:zero] and nums[zero+1:] slices make unnecessary O(n) copies; a single loop skipping the zero index would suffice. The match statement is stylistically heavy for three simple branches, and the division approach ignores the follow-up's no-division challenge.
complexity.summary: Counts zeros and branches: multiple zeros yield all zeros; exactly one zero yields the product of non-zero elements placed at the zero index; otherwise divides the total product by each element. Division is exact since every element divides the total product, so floor division is safe even with negatives.

complexity.notes: The `size < 1` guard is dead code given the stated constraint sz >= 1, but harmless. A one-pass fast/slow-pointer version would avoid the second traversal but has the same asymptotics.
complexity.summary: Two-pass approach: first count the list length L, then walk L-n steps from a dummy head to land on the node before the target and splice it out, handling head removal via the dummy.

complexity.notes: The O(n) array of node references is simple and correct, though the classic O(1)-space approach (find middle, reverse second half, merge) avoids the extra storage. The branching inside the pointer loop is slightly convoluted but handles both even and odd lengths correctly.
complexity.summary: Collect all nodes into an array, then use two pointers from both ends to rewire next pointers into the interleaved order, terminating the new tail with None.

complexity.notes: Handles the 0/1-node base cases up front; the standard three-pointer while-loop formulation is slightly more idiomatic, but this variant is correct.
complexity.summary: Iterative in-place reversal: walks the list once, redirecting each node's next pointer to its predecessor, with the final node becoming the new head.

complexity.notes: Works but unidiomatic: the standard iterative reversal uses three pointers (prev, curr) in O(1) space, avoiding both the array and the clever-but-fragile nodes[-1]/nodes[-2] indexing. The O(n) extra space is unnecessary.
complexity.summary: Collects all nodes into an array by walking the list, then rewrites each node's next pointer to point at its predecessor by indexing the array, returning the former tail. The trailing None appended during the walk conveniently serves as the new tail's next via nodes[-1].

complexity.notes: Concise and readable; correctness hinges on the delimiter lying outside the 256-character ASCII set, so it would not survive the follow-up's arbitrary-Unicode generalization. A length-prefixed encoding would be more robust.
complexity.summary: Joins the strings with a non-ASCII emoji delimiter (appended after the last string too), then decodes via split and drops the trailing empty fragment; the empty-list case maps to the empty string, which decodes back to [].

complexity.correctness_reason: The delimiter is composed of ASCII characters that input strings may legally contain, so e.g. strs = ["xpaysutdlfmywvaugplk49w87ky9v478y"] encodes and then decodes into extra spurious segments, failing round-trip on a permitted input.
complexity.notes: The delimiter trick is fragile; a length-prefixed encoding (e.g. 'len#str') is the standard robust approach and equally simple.
complexity.summary: Joins the list with a hard-coded 'random' delimiter string (appending it at the end) and decodes via split plus a pop of the trailing empty segment. Time and space are linear in total character volume.

complexity.notes: decode could be O(n) by keeping an integer index into s instead of repeatedly doing s = s[...:] (each slice copies the remainder, making the loop O(total^2)). Using str.index per step is also less idiomatic than scanning with a pointer. Encode itself is clean and O(total chars).
complexity.summary: Length-prefix encoding: each string is written as `<len>|<content>`, and decode repeatedly finds the next `|`, parses the length, and slices out that many characters. Decode is quadratic because each iteration re-slices the entire remaining string.

complexity.notes: The per-count linear scan over num_counts.items() plus the final set() dedup are awkward workarounds; collecting (count, key) pairs and taking the k largest directly (e.g. heapq.nlargest) would be cleaner and avoid both. Sorting all m counts is O(m log m) when only the top k are needed.
complexity.summary: Counts frequencies in a dict, sorts the frequency values and takes the k largest, then scans the dict once per selected count to collect matching keys, deduplicating via set at the end.

complexity.notes: Unidiomatic and convoluted: sorting loses the indices, forcing linear .index() calls and a fragile pop-and-shift trick for the duplicate-value case; sorting (value, index) pairs or a one-pass hash map would be cleaner, and the hash map version runs in O(n).
complexity.summary: Sorts a copy of nums, then uses two pointers to find the pair of values summing to target, and recovers their original indices via nums.index (with a pop-based fixup when the two values are equal).

adversarial.note: n distinct multiples of 2**61-1 (already ascending), all hashing to 0, so every dict insert/lookup collides

complexity.notes: Re-sorting ignores the given sorted precondition and violates the required O(1) extra space; a plain two-pointer pass on the original array would give O(n) time and O(1) space. The repeated nums.index() calls are O(n) each but only run a constant number of times, so they don't change the asymptotics.
complexity.summary: Sorts a copy of the array, runs a two-pointer scan on the sorted copy to find the two values, then recovers the original 1-indexed positions with index() lookups (with a pop-based fixup when both values are equal).

complexity.notes: Using valid *= isValidLine(...) (boolean coercion through integer multiplication) instead of valid &= ... or an early return is an odd idiom, and it prevents short-circuiting; list.count inside a loop is also less clear than a set-based duplicate check, though both are constant here.
complexity.summary: Extracts each of the 9 rows, 9 columns, and 9 sub-boxes as flat lists and validates each by checking that no non-'.' cell appears more than once via list.count. The board is structurally fixed at 9x9, so all work is constant.

complexity.notes: Membership test against a 3-element list is constant-time; a dict mapping closers to openers would be more idiomatic. Note each elif pops exactly once, so control flow is correct.
complexity.summary: Classic stack-based validation: push each opening bracket, and on a closing bracket pop the stack and verify it matches the corresponding opener; the string is valid iff no mismatch occurs and the stack is empty at the end.

complexity.notes: Clean and idiomatic; the map keys come from a fixed 3-character set, so hashing is bounded and lookups are O(1) even in the worst case.
complexity.summary: Single pass with a stack: push opening brackets, and on each closing bracket pop and check it matches via a fixed close-to-open map; valid iff the stack is empty at the end and no mismatch occurred.
